book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

chapters.relation: Lisle tests Klosterman's sports essays with Gadamer's hermeneutics: interpreters bring cultural 'prejudices' to a text (the '86 Celtics, soccer, gridiron football) in an open dialogue the text can resist. He argues Klosterman's soccer essay fails as interpretation — it builds a totalitarian-sport thesis ('Mussolini... Khmer Rouge') on his Wyndmere youth baseball coaching grievance, whacking a straw man the text never endorses. The 'Football' essay fares better, but its claim that the read option proves the game's hidden liberality is undercut by the play's 1950s lineage (Arthur Daley's keep-or-give option, Bud Wilkinson's Split-T, Belichick's 'single wing') and by Walter Camp's Taylorist codification of football as managed bureaucracy versus soccer's horizontal, player-driven flow.

Brooks argues Klosterman is an unacknowledged heir of McLuhan's media ecology: his Fargo Rock City account of hair metal's rise through FM radio, metal magazines, and MTV's 'collective unconscious,' Britney Spears as a low-definition 'cool medium' everyone rebrands, and the 'singular club scene' as global village all do media-ecology work. But Brooks docks him fifteen percent for clinging to an authenticity fantasy — the Unabomber-essay claim that technology makes us 'never been less human' — which McLuhan's dictum that 'there is absolutely no inevitability as long as there is a willingness to contemplate what is happening' refutes. In Rorty's spirit of persuading by joshing rather than arguing, he challenges Klosterman to drop the ontology and turn his interpretive powers on real problems like compassion fatigue and Darfur.

Reisch treats Klosterman's Jack-and-Jane hypothetical (Jane dumps Jack because he watched a woman masturbate) as a trap Otto Neurath called pseudorationalism: in ethics we invent objective-sounding rational laws ('thou shalt not watch thy neighbor masturbate') that collapse under counterexamples about porn, Madonna, and zoo baboons, since only logic and math sustain such systems. The defensible breakup would rest on honest personal reasons — the incident shaking Jane's faith in Jack's commitment — not a nonexistent cosmic rule; the chapter closes by imagining Jane escaping pseudorationalism in 2008 and realizing what her 2005 decision was really worth.

Framed by Dick's wait in a Klosterman signing line, the chapter asks how a critic acquires rock-star power. Plato's Ion supplies the magnet chain of inspiration (muse, poet, rhapsode, spectator), which puts Klosterman near the spectator end — he 'only got to second base' with the muse Thalia until Downtown Owl. Nietzsche's master and slave moralities then explain the critic's ascent: Klosterman is the cunning slave-priest who seizes power from warrior-artists through wit and articulate opinion, exactly as priestly values overthrew warrior values. Dick half-endorses the diagnosis, admits he prefers the slave's world of safety, and concludes that power — even the power to sell books and pay rent — is how we stay alive.

Fitzpatrick asks whether Klosterman's low-culture project (tribute bands, Toby Keith, the McNuggets diet) is mere titillation or genuinely valuable. Bentham's pushpin-versus-poetry hedonism matches Klosterman's rejection of 'guilty pleasures,' while Aristotle's eudaimonia — and Plato's forms, on which a tribute band is a copy of a copy of a copy — condemns a life of amusement. Mill resolves the question twice over: higher and lower pleasures justify ranking Klosterman's contemplative criticism above mere sensation, and On Liberty's free market of ideas shows that even false or partial low-culture claims (about Garth Brooks, Spurlock's Super Size Me) keep high culture's truths from decaying into unexamined dogma.

Mistich and McCullough read Klosterman's desire essays through the psychoanalytic-philosophical tradition. 'This Is Emo' — 'No woman will ever satisfy me' — is glossed with Žižek, Lacan, and Butler: desire is not meant to be fulfilled, and satisfaction would only kill it, so Klosterman's failed Waldorf Astoria romance is structurally inevitable. Kojève's Hegelian thesis that all desire is desire for the other's recognition explains Billy Joel's tragic craving for rock-critic canonization, the cereal-box hunger to be 'cool,' and Klosterman's three-week ultimatum to Diane, while Freud's theory of fantasy shows how pop culture (Lloyd Dobler, internet porn) scripts the romantic and sexual desires it then frustrates.

Vosen answers Klosterman's hyperthetical about cats that suddenly read at a twelfth-grade level against his implied expectation: they would love Garfield rather than find it an insulting caricature. Reading the strip through Dan Walsh's Garfield-minus-Garfield project, she argues the comics reveal that Garfield is the glue keeping Jon Arbuckle from a full existential breakdown, so literate cats would find hope, renewed purpose, and the comfort that life could always be worse — they could be Jon. The exercise turns a throwaway joke into a small meditation on meaninglessness, comparison, and what keeps a life from collapsing.

Vannatta reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture — the Left Behind novels, Victory TV's Steven, Kurt Warner's Super Bowl, Jesus Camp — as living Puritan Calvinism: original sin (Klosterman's cruel third-graders), justification by faith alone, unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest'), and predestination that leaves uncertain whether our actions matter in the divine equation. The chapter's pivot is truth versus peace: Puritan-born-again certainty sacrifices peace for antecedent truth, from the 1675 Massachusetts settlements to Robertson and Falwell on 9/11. Against this Vannatta sets the pragmatist alternative — truth as the outcome of communal inquiry in service of peaceful living — recasting God as the web of relationships and dissolving his own childhood camp's contradiction between 'I'm Third' and its cult of competition.

Priebe builds a tongue-in-cheek 'Chuckism,' showing that Klosterman's books accidentally supply every element of a religion's formula: a bearded dude-deity, scripture, interpretive community, rules, and an afterlife (heaven as an always-neon Las Vegas, earthly life as purgatory sized by SIDS and 102-year-olds, plus a theory of reincarnation). Her ten commandments — thou shalt rock, swear, name-drop, be illogical, use footnotes — are mined from his actual writing style and its deliberate bad syllogisms. Under the blasphemy sits a serious claim: religion's structure is arbitrary and its orthodoxy enforceable, while Chuck's creed that 'living is dying, little by little' and 'life is tourism' answers the meaning-of-life question the older faiths evade.

Fitzpatrick uses Klosterman's hyperthetical — kick a shackled Clydesdale to death in twenty minutes and every political prisoner on earth goes free — to stage the consequentialism-versus-non-consequentialism dispute. He argues the scenario's framing (a warm, cuddly horse) rigs it for the anti-consequentialist, but once you grant that Amnesty International's prisoners suffer worse than the horse — the tortured Syrian teenage protestor is his example — the question becomes whether one awful act to a horse is permissible to prevent worse suffering to many humans. His only remaining hesitation is practical: could you actually finish the job in twenty minutes?

Klosterman's own epilogue responds to being philosophized about: he understands the book exists because he is 'famous enough' to sell philosophy to readers who do not buy philosophy, and that its favorite source, Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs, is his least logical book — which is exactly why it sold. He diagnoses his central tension (entertaining writing about unsolvable ideas, consumed by audiences who want only one half), admits via the Lennon 'the pseuds will love it' anecdote that he is an unreliable narrator writing willfully misleading art, and disclaims any intent to persuade anyone of anything. A footnote concedes the chapter on McLuhan that he absorbed McLuhan's ideas 'by accident,' while disputing that the problem of authenticity has been solved — the through-line of his claim that all fifteen hundred pages of his work are about the difference between the 'real' and 'reality.'

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: Hermeneutic philosopher of Truth and Method who held that all understanding proceeds from the interpreter's culturally inherited prejudices in an open dialogue with the text.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire framework — sport as cultural text, Klosterman's prejudices, interpretations that shift yet can be definitively false — is Gadamer's hermeneutics applied to the '86 Celtics, soccer, and gridiron football.

holes.name: Philosophical Hermeneutics
holes.what: The theory that meaning emerges from a fluid dialogue between interpreter and text, in which neither side is fixed and the text can challenge or resist its readings.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues Klosterman's soccer interpretation is an erroneous dialogue-thwarting reading while his football reading partly succeeds — a hermeneutic evaluation of pop-cultural interpretation.

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who founded media ecology, arguing media environments (the global village, hot and cool media, figure-ground) reshape perception and society.
holes.why: Chapter 25 claims Klosterman is a twenty-first-century McLuhan whose analyses of metal, Britney Spears, and laugh tracks borrow McLuhan's concepts without acknowledgment.

holes.name: Media Ecology (the medium is the message)
holes.what: The study of whole media environments as systems that quietly structure human identity, culture, and experience, rather than evaluating individual media products.
holes.why: Chapter 25's thesis is that Klosterman is a (85 percent) media ecologist doing big-picture analysis of how radio, MTV, and magazines converge to reshape culture.

holes.name: Otto Neurath
holes.what: Logical-empiricist philosopher of science who warned that 'pseudorationalism' misapplies rational frameworks beyond logic and mathematics, where they inevitably fail.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Klosterman's Jack-and-Jane breakup hypothetical as an instance of the pseudorationalism trap Neurath identified in ethical reasoning.

holes.name: Pseudorationalism
holes.what: The false belief that messy human domains like ethics can be governed by objective rational rules, leading us to defend fabricated moral laws with endless ad hoc qualifications.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues everyone judging Jack and Jane is a pseudorationalist propping up a nonexistent cosmic rule against watching masturbation, instead of giving honest personal reasons.

holes.name: Platonic Inspiration (the Ion's magnet)
holes.what: Plato's theory in the Ion that poetic creation is divine possession transmitted like magnetism down a chain — muse to poet to rhapsode to spectator — rather than a knowable craft.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses the magnet chain to ask whether Klosterman is an inspired artist or merely a powerful spectator-critic several links removed from the muse.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who theorized fantasy (day-dreaming) as wish-fulfillment that substitutes for ungratified desire from childhood onward.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses Freud's 'Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming' to argue pop-cultural fantasies (Lloyd Dobler, internet porn) are the condition that makes Klosterman's desires possible.

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst whose dictum 'do not cede on your desire' and theory of constitutive lack frame desire as inherently unsatisfiable and self-reproducing.
holes.why: Chapter 30 reads Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' as a pseudo-Lacanian text in which satisfaction would only foreclose desire, making unfulfillment structural rather than accidental.

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher-psychoanalyst who popularizes Lacan through pop culture, arguing the realization of desire coincides with its reproduction, not its fulfillment.
holes.why: Chapter 30 leans on Žižek's Looking Awry (the 'desire to desire,' fantasy staging desire as such) and his Star Wars Holiday Special example to gloss Klosterman's romantic failures.

holes.name: Fantasy and Desire (psychoanalytic theory of desire)
holes.what: The psychoanalytic thesis that fantasy is the imagined scene which makes desire possible and keeps it circulating, while desire itself aims at recognition and is never fulfilled.
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues pop culture produces the fantasies that frame Klosterman's romantic appetites, and that his (and Billy Joel's) desire is really a desire to be recognized.

holes.name: John Calvin
holes.what: Reformation theologian whose doctrines of predestination, justification by faith alone, vocational calling, and unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest') defined Puritanism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture (Left Behind, Kurt Warner, Jesus Camp) as Calvinist Puritanism, needing Calvin's election, calling, and truth-trumps-peace theology for the argument.
